%% -- Abstract --
\begin{abstract}
Metamorphic testing helps test programs when direct test oracles are unavailable, but identifying metamorphic relations (MRs) remains largely experience- or search-driven. We study MR identification, not average fault-detection superiority, for operator-algebraic program families. We introduce \textbf{NOETHER}, a two-level framework that curates a program-family operator algebra, decomposes it into recurrent structural components, and mechanically derives MR classes / MetaPatterns through \texttt{CONSTRUCT-MP}. The construction makes MR origin and applicability boundaries explicit, proves closure of the downstream derivation, and gives an \emph{Invariance-Blindness Theorem} characterising detectable and undetectable faults for the symmetry and self-adjoint MetaPatterns within the stated fault class. Across expert/search-derived MR corpora, three algebra instantiations, 21 in-scope real faults, and a 20-mutant equivariant-ML study, NOETHER maps real faults to 8 of 10 MR families, detects 7/20 mutants versus 2/20 for a large-language-model-prompted set and 0/20 for a literature set, and identifies five obstructions bounding the current \texttt{Translate} signature. The replication package releases supplementary material, prompts, raw outputs, mappings, and scripts.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Metamorphic Testing (MT), introduced by Chen et~al.\ in 1998~\cite{Chen1998}, was admitted into the IEEE/ISO/IEC software-testing standards in 2022~\cite{ISO29119} and is now used for testing artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning (ML) systems~\cite{Segura2016, LiTOSEM2025}. Its central artefact is the \emph{metamorphic relation} (MR): a property that constrains how a program's outputs must covary across multiple executions, thereby substituting for an explicit oracle in domains where one cannot exist. Despite MT's maturity, MR identification, the task of deciding \emph{which} properties hold for a program under test, remains its binding constraint. Practitioners report three recurring difficulties: high dependence on tester domain knowledge, mutually incompatible MR formulations for the same program, and low reuse of MR sets across teams or projects~\cite{Segura2016, LiTOSEM2025}. Recent work has responded at the application layer, by mining MRs for particular domains, and at the integration layer, by automating search through evolutionary, mining-based, or large-language-model (LLM)-assisted pipelines~\cite{MRScout2024, GenMorph2024, Shin2024}. The foundational layer has not advanced at the same pace.

The principal artefact at that foundational layer is the \emph{MetaPattern} (MP): an equivalence class over MRs that captures a recurrent structural strategy a tester invokes when reasoning about program properties. MetaPatterns organise the otherwise unbounded MR design space into a small, interpretable scaffold; methods that exploit them, including the structured MR identification approaches METRIC~\cite{ChenMETRIC2016} and METRIC+~\cite{SunMETRICplus2021}, and the recent wave of LLM-prompted MR generators, depend on the scaffold's quality. Yet across the literature, MetaPattern catalogues are still grounded mainly in induction over observed examples. A typical proposal lists $k$ patterns drawn from cluster analysis or expert codification, demonstrates that the patterns ``cover'' some corpus of MRs to a target threshold, and stops. This leaves a foundational \emph{origin--closure--transferability gap}: without a structural source, there is no clear boundary on what the pattern space contains; without a transfer rule, a relation written for one program rarely moves cleanly to another, even when both programs share a deep structural template.

None of the existing MP proposals, including prior work on five reactor-physics patterns, answers the three questions that any structural account of MetaPatterns should answer:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Origin.} \emph{Why} exactly these MetaPatterns and not others? What is the structural source of an MP, as distinct from an empirical regularity in the corpus on which it was induced?
  \item \textbf{Closure.} Under what mathematical conditions is a discovered MP set \emph{closed under a stated derivation operator}, in the sense that it is guaranteed not to miss patterns reachable through the operator from a structurally fixed input? Absolute completeness over all properties one might write over the underlying structure is a strictly stronger demand and remains open in general.
  \item \textbf{Transferability.} When the program family changes (from reactor physics to natural-language inference, from numerical libraries to recommender systems), how does the MetaPattern set change, and can the new set be obtained without re-running the entire empirical induction in the new domain?
\end{enumerate}

This paper proposes such a structural source for a deliberately bounded class of systems: operator-algebraic program families, i.e., equation-governed or relational-semantics families whose behaviour can be represented through operators, invariants, and equivalence-preserving transformations. We introduce \textbf{NOETHER}, a constructive framework that derives MetaPatterns from the operator-algebraic structure of the program family under test. The framework extracts MetaPatterns from invariants of an operator algebra $\mathcal{A}_P$ (formally defined in Section~\ref{sec:prelim}) that captures the program family's mathematical scaffolding. Given $\mathcal{A}_P$, NOETHER produces a MetaPattern set $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ (constructed by the algorithm of Section~\ref{sec:framework}) together with a closure guarantee over the algebra-induced MR space. Given a different program family with a different algebra $\mathcal{A}_{P'}$, the same construction produces $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_{P'})$ without re-running empirical induction over observed MRs.

The name is deliberate but limited. Noether's first theorem is useful here only as a methodological analogy: a catalogue of observed invariants can sometimes be replaced by a derivation grounded in structure.\footnote{The theorem appeared in Noether's 1918 paper \emph{Invariante Variationsprobleme}, addressing a question Hilbert and Klein had raised about energy conservation in general relativity. We do not invoke it as a theorem about programs: program semantics and metamorphic relations do not provide an action functional. The analogy is methodological only.} The replacement does not eliminate empirical work; it lifts the empirical step from per-instance enumeration to per-domain structural identification, one cycle of induction per stable domain rather than per program. In NOETHER, domain experts must still distil $\mathcal{A}_P$ from program semantics, and Section~\ref{sec:threats-limitations} states this limitation explicitly. What becomes algebraic is the downstream step from $\mathcal{A}_P$ to the MetaPattern set. Figure~\ref{fig:noether-arch} summarises the architecture.

We make five MR-identification contributions. The load-bearing theoretical result is an Invariance-Blindness Theorem (IBT): a falsifiable characterisation of which implementation faults an algebra-derived MR can and cannot detect, distinct from the intentionally modest by-construction closure guarantee.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{C1 (framework).} We introduce NOETHER, a \emph{layered} MR-identification framework for operator-algebraic program families: the upstream layer empirically curates a program-family operator algebra and structural decomposition (Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:seven-blocks}; partly distilled from a pressurized-water-reactor (PWR) MR corpus, \S\ref{subsec:reactor-mapping}), while the downstream \texttt{CONSTRUCT-MP} layer mechanically derives five MetaPatterns and ten MR families from that algebra.
  \item \textbf{C2 (theory).} We give a three-part theory for the algebra-induced MR space. Theorem~1 proves a \emph{no-drop closure invariant}: every \texttt{Translate}-reachable MR over $\mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_{P})$ is assigned to a canonical structural component and MetaPattern class. Theorem~2 gives polynomial-time constructibility under a finite generating set. The negative result refutes absolute completeness on $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PWR}}$ with two safety-analysis MRs and five pairwise-independent obstructions in \texttt{Translate}'s signature (\S\ref{subsec:negative-pwr}, Appendix~\ref{app:negative-proofs}); these obstructions are part of the contribution because they identify MR classes the current construction should not claim to reach. The Invariance-Blindness Theorem (\S\ref{subsec:ibt}) characterises exactly which implementation faults the $G$ and $T^{*}$ MetaPatterns can and cannot detect within the stated linear fault class.
  \item \textbf{C3 (canonical symbol system).} Instantiating NOETHER on a real program family maps a literature-derived PWR MR corpus onto one canonical vocabulary: five MetaPatterns, two family-layer refinements, one relational extension, and the ten MR-family symbols of Table~\ref{tab:mr-families}. The same symbols are used throughout the theory, figures, evidence tables, and discussion, including the deflationary comparison to Murphy et al.'s six ML classes~\cite{Murphy2008} (\S\ref{subsec:pmcm-worked}).
  \item \textbf{C4 (transferability).} We demonstrate \emph{structural} transferability, not empirical superiority, by instantiating NOETHER on three structurally distinct algebras: Boltzmann reactor physics (\S\ref{sec:reactor}), equivariant ML (\S\ref{sec:cross-domain}), and relational query optimisers (\S\ref{subsec:third-domain}), the last exercising the relational extension beyond the Lie-group / self-adjoint / time-reversal core.
  \item \textbf{C5 (evidence protocol).} We define an MR-identification evidence protocol around RQ1--RQ4: canonical coverage, origin/boundary explanation, cross-domain and real-fault recurrence, and secondary executability/blind-spot checks. The empirical evidence includes expert/search-derived MR corpora, 21 real scientific-computing faults mapped to 8 of 10 MR families, and an equivariant-ML mutation study in which the NOETHER-derived set detects 7/20 mutants versus 2/20 for an LLM-prompted set and 0/20 for a literature set. These results are used as executability, complementarity, and blind-spot evidence, not average-superiority evidence. A replication package releases the supplementary material, prompts, raw outputs, mapping files, and scripts needed to inspect or rerun the reported checks.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Scope and adoption value.} This paper evaluates \emph{MR identification} for operator-algebraic program families: whether a method can derive structurally justified MR classes from a program family's governing equations or relational semantics. It does not evaluate MR \emph{effectiveness} in the sense of average fault-detection rate, mutation score, or general defect-revealing superiority. The five MetaPatterns (with two refinements and a relational extension) are curated by inspecting mathematical structures that recur across the program families we have studied; they are not derived from an algebraic axiom. The framework therefore has two layers: an \emph{upstream layer} (curating $\mathcal{A}_P$ and its structural decomposition) that remains empirical and human, and a \emph{downstream layer} (mechanically deriving $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ from $\mathcal{A}_P$) that is algorithmic and provable. NOETHER's intended practical value is not to replace search-based MR generators in every setting, but to give high-structure domains an auditable source for MR families, a transferable symbol system, predictable blind spots, and a structural prior that can complement search, mining, or LLM-prompted generation.

\paragraph{Upstream modelling effort.} NOETHER moves, rather than eliminates, one part of the identification burden. The upstream modelling task is to collect the governing equations or semantic rewrite rules, name the operators exposed by those equations, assign them to the current structural components, and record which program-interface controls and observations make the resulting family executable. The case studies report the downstream cost once $\mathcal{A}_P$ is available, but they do not establish a general human-effort distribution for algebra distillation; this remains a limitation and a measurement target for future work. The claim of this paper is therefore bounded: once a program-family algebra has been curated, CONSTRUCT-MP gives a closed, auditable derivation of the algebra-induced MR space and exposes the boundary of the current \texttt{Translate} signature.

The remainder of the paper follows a TOSEM-style method-paper structure. Section~\ref{sec:related} reviews expert MR design, structured taxonomies, and search-based MR generation. Section~\ref{sec:noether-framework} presents the NOETHER method, the two-level model from identified MR class to executable MR instance, the structural-component taxonomy, and the coverage rules. Section~\ref{sec:experiments} defines RQ1--RQ4 and the evidence protocol. Section~\ref{sec:results-discussion} reports canonical coverage, origin/boundary explanation, cross-domain and real-fault recurrence, and RQ4 executability/blind-spot checks. Section~\ref{sec:threats-limitations} discusses threats to validity and limitations. Section~\ref{sec:future-work} states future work; Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

We organise prior work along four lines: MT/MR fundamentals and the long-standing identification bottleneck; structured MR identification through category, specification, and model scaffolds; automated MR identification through mining, search, learning, and LLM assistance; and MetaPattern catalogues, including a prior reactor-physics taxonomy. These lines differ in mechanism, but they share one limitation: their pattern structures are induced from observed MRs, mined artefacts, or manually supplied models rather than derived from the mathematical structure that makes those MRs hold.

\subsection{Metamorphic testing and the MR identification bottleneck}

Metamorphic Testing was introduced by Chen, Cheung, and Yiu in 1998 to address the test-oracle problem~\cite{Chen1998}, a general obstacle in software testing when expected outputs cannot be automatically determined~\cite{Barr2015OracleProblem}. An MR is a logical implication of the form $R_i(x_1,\dots,x_n) \Rightarrow R_o(P(x_1),\dots,P(x_n))$, where $P$ is the program under test, $R_i$ is an input relation, and $R_o$ is an output relation. When $R_i$ holds but $R_o$ fails on actual executions, a fault is reported, without any need to know the absolute correct output of any single execution. Over two decades MT has become standard equipment for testing systems whose oracles are otherwise inaccessible: scientific computing, machine learning classifiers, autonomous vehicles, search engines, compilers, and large language models~\cite{Segura2016, LiTOSEM2025}.

The community has long acknowledged a single binding constraint on MT's effectiveness: MR identification. Surveys spanning twenty years agree that identifying high-quality MRs requires (i) deep familiarity with the program's functional semantics, (ii) substantive domain background (physical, mathematical, or linguistic, depending on the system), and (iii) the ability to convert that background into executable property assertions~\cite{Segura2016, LiTOSEM2025}. Liu et al.~\cite{Liu2014MTEffectiveness} provide the canonical empirical evidence that even ad-hoc MRs detect a substantial fraction of mutants given modest tester training, while Murphy et al.~\cite{Murphy2008} catalogued the structural properties of ML applications relevant to MR design and Xie et al.~\cite{Xie2011} demonstrated that MT scales effectively to supervised classifiers. Testers without sufficient domain background tend to identify only ``trivial MRs''. A 2024 survey explicitly identifies AI assistance, especially via large language models, as the most promising open avenue for closing the identification gap~\cite{LiTOSEM2025}; Saha and Kanewala~\cite{Saha2019SupervisedMR} report that, on a benchmark of 709 mutants for supervised classifiers, current MR sets detect only 14.8\%, which exposes the gap.

The bottleneck is also structural: even when MRs are identified, the field has accumulated little consensus on \emph{how} they are identified. Different authors confront the same program and produce dissimilar MR sets. Once written, an MR rarely migrates: a relation drafted for one ML classifier seldom transports to another, and a relation drafted for one numerical solver seldom transports across solver families.

\subsection{Structured MR identification}

Structured MR identification has already moved the field away from ad hoc relation design. METRIC organises MR construction around an ``input/output category'' framework: the tester first identifies relevant categories of input transformations and output relations, then composes MRs from category pairs~\cite{ChenMETRIC2016}. METRIC+ extends this scheme by enriching the category catalogue and providing systematic combination rules that reduce the human burden in category enumeration~\cite{SunMETRICplus2021}. Other structured lines instantiate the scaffold through domain or artefact models: Segura et al.\ define MR patterns for query-based systems from recurrent query features and explicitly use relational algebra as the vocabulary for those patterns~\cite{Segura2019QBSMRPatterns}; Li et al.\ construct MRs from tabular-expression specifications~\cite{Li2020TabularMR}; Yan et al.\ decompose the input side of scientific-computing MRs into basic input-pattern structures~\cite{Yan2022InputPattern}; and Lin et al.\ organise scientific-software MRs hierarchically~\cite{Lin2018HierarchicalMR}. Together, these approaches remain the strongest existing attempt to give MR identification an explicit scaffold.

Our disagreement is not with this direction but with its grounding. The categories, patterns, tables, and input decompositions are introduced through expert curation, artefact-specific structure, or observed reuse, and are validated by empirical coverage on benchmark programs. This leaves two of our three foundational questions unanswered. \emph{Origin}: existing structured methods do not derive their categories from program-level operator algebra. Even query-based MR patterns use relational algebra as an organising vocabulary, not as a closed derivation system whose primitive structural components define an MR design space. \emph{Closure}: these frameworks do not provide a mathematical condition under which the category set is complete; coverage is reported but not proved. The third question, \emph{transferability}, is only partially addressed. The same category templates can be invoked across domains, but because the categories are not algebraically bound to specific program structures, transfer rests on an assumption of universality that remains open.

\subsection{Automated MR identification}

Automated MR identification attacks the bottleneck by searching for executable relations more directly. Early search and dynamic-inference work includes likely metamorphic-property inference from executions~\cite{Su2015LikelyMR}, search-based inference of polynomial MRs~\cite{Zhang2014PolynomialMR}, and AutoMR's discovery and cleansing of numerical MRs through search plus redundancy reduction~\cite{Zhang2019AutoMR}. MR-Scout mines MRs from existing test suites by extracting input-transformation and output-assertion patterns from test-case pairs and abstracting them into reusable relations~\cite{MRScout2024}. GenMorph evolves MR candidates through genetic programming, co-evolving input transformations with output assertions and using mutation-killing as the fitness signal~\cite{GenMorph2024}. Shin et~al.\ derive executable MRs from natural-language requirements through few-shot prompting of a large language model, with validation through an industrial questionnaire study with Siemens~\cite{Shin2024}; further LLM-assisted variants, including ChatGPT-driven MR generation~\cite{ZhangChatGPTMR2023}, domain-customised GPTs for autonomous-driving simulators~\cite{GPTMR2025}, and multi-agent retrieval-augmented pipelines for traffic-rule MRs~\cite{AutoMT2025}, extend this template into safety-critical or rule-rich domains. Within ML-system testing, differential-testing approaches such as DeepXplore~\cite{DeepXplore2017} use input-transformation invariance as a proxy oracle, complementary to the explicit MR formulation we adopt here.

A second strand uses program-structure, specification, documentation, or model features rather than test-case mining. Kanewala et al.~\cite{Kanewala2016GraphKernel} predict MRs of scientific software via graph-kernel learning over control-flow and data-dependency graphs, an early demonstration that program structure carries enough signal for automated MR discovery. MeMo extracts equivalence MRs from Javadoc comments~\cite{Blasi2021MeMo}. Nolasco et al.'s MemoRIA~\cite{Nolasco2024MemoRIA} infers MRs by deriving an object-protocol abstraction and validating candidates through fuzzing plus SAT-based reduction, then evaluates on 22 Java subjects. Clark et al.\ generate MRs from causal graphs, making model misspecification an explicit boundary of the method~\cite{Clark2023CausalMT}. Tao et al.'s Mettoc~\cite{Tao2010Mettoc} applied MT to compiler testing using equivalence-preservation as the canonical relation. Ying et al.~\cite{Ying2025MRPatterns} formalise relationships between metamorphic-relation patterns into family trees, and Altamimi et al.~\cite{Altamimi2022MRSLR} provide a recent systematic literature review of MR-automation work that catalogues the structural-vs-empirical-search divide our framework targets. Earlier LLM-assisted attempts include Zhang et al.~\cite{ZhangChatGPTMR2023} on ChatGPT-driven MR generation.

Each of these methods automates a different part of MR identification, but all treat the MR space as an empirical, artefact-derived, or model-supplied search space. MR-Scout's recall is bounded by the relations already latent in existing tests. Search-based and evolutionary methods can discover useful numerical or executable MRs, but the reported cleansing and redundancy-reduction steps follow from the search representation rather than from an account of the mathematical origin of the surviving relations. GenMorph's evolutionary search is shaped by the mutation-killing fitness function. LLM-prompted approaches are sensitive to prompt phrasing when no structural prior constrains generation. Documentation-, protocol-, and causal-model-based methods are more interpretable, but their boundary is the supplied artefact or model rather than a program-family operator algebra. None of these methods can state, before search begins, which MR types lie outside its reach, because none has an algebraic account of the space being searched. The tradeoff is explicit: NOETHER requires a stronger upstream domain model and is less automatic at the start, but it supplies algebraic warrant, closure, and non-reachability information. It should therefore be read as a structural prior and audit layer for high-structure domains, not as a replacement for mining, search, or LLM prompting.

The intuition that symmetries furnish partial oracles predates this work. Gotlieb's symmetric testing treats input permutations whose outputs must agree as a checkable oracle~\cite{Gotlieb2003Symmetries}, and a follow-up study models its test quality on Java Card APIs~\cite{GotliebBernard2006}. Patel and Hierons survey such oracle strategies for non-testable systems~\cite{PatelHierons2018}, while Khritankov and Iakusheva systematically review metamorphic-relation derivation and group the recurring input transformations into six families~\cite{KhritankovIakusheva2024}. In machine learning, related symmetry notions are studied empirically: Gruver et al.\ measure how much equivariance a trained network actually acquires~\cite{Gruver2023LieDerivative}, and Kaba et al.\ attain equivariance by learning canonicalization functions rather than constraining the architecture~\cite{Kaba2023Canonicalization}. These lines name and exploit the symmetry-oracle intuition, yet each identifies relations per program, surveys them descriptively, or approximates symmetry inside a model. None derive metamorphic patterns algorithmically from the governing equations of a program family. NOETHER does not invent the symmetry layer; its contribution is a constructive derivation over the structural-component layer, together with closure and complexity results and a domain-transferable skeleton. In that setting, the symmetry oracle becomes a construction rule rather than a per-program insight.

\subsection{MetaPattern catalogues and empirical adequacy}

MetaPattern catalogues organise the post-hoc inventory of identified MRs into a smaller vocabulary of recurring strategies. Such catalogues typically result from clustering observed MRs, codifying expert intuitions about ``kinds of properties testers reason about'', and validating the catalogue's coverage on a benchmark MR corpus. Reactor-physics test suites have produced taxonomies of conservation, monotonicity, convergence, trajectory, and partial-order patterns~\cite{BellGlasstone1970, LewisMiller1993}; Zhou et al.~\cite{Zhou2020SymmetryMRP} introduced an explicit \emph{symmetry metamorphic relation pattern} as a reusable abstraction for deriving concrete MRs across applications; Lin et al.~\cite{Lin2018HierarchicalMR} proposed hierarchical MRs for scientific software; Ying et al.~\cite{Ying2025MRPatterns} formalises the relationships between MR patterns into \emph{family trees} with explicit refinement and specialisation edges, and reports a state-of-the-art (SOTA) pattern hierarchy that organises previously proposed patterns into a single classification structure. The most recent state-of-the-art survey of MR generation~\cite{LiTOSEM2025} maps the field's twenty-year output across pattern catalogues, mining, evolutionary search, and LLM-prompted methods. Adequacy frameworks such as the Pattern--Matrix Coverage Metric, and recent MT adequacy work based on MRs and source inputs~\cite{Fu2024MTAdequacy}, assess how thoroughly a given test suite or MR set occupies an already-defined testing space. They do not define coverage over the structural components that give rise to MR classes.

Ying et al.'s family-tree formalism~\cite{Ying2025MRPatterns} is the closest published cousin: both organise MR patterns into a hierarchy, but Ying et al.'s family tree is a refinement/specialisation tree rooted in informally-named categories (symmetry, additive, multiplicative), whereas NOETHER's MetaPatterns are quotients of the algebra-induced MR space $\mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ under structural equivalence (Definition~\ref{def:alg-induced}), each derived from a specific structural component. A family-tree node maps to one or more NOETHER MetaPatterns when it admits an operator-algebraic specification (Ying et al.'s ``symmetry'' node splits into $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$ and $m_{\mathrm{adj}}$), while $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ has no family-tree counterpart; the two are complementary, Ying et al.\ cataloguing inductively at the MR-instance level and NOETHER providing the algebraic warrant per pattern.

Such catalogues are useful, but each is, by construction, an empirical artefact. None of the existing catalogues can answer the three foundational questions of Section~\ref{sec:intro}.

\subsection{Convergent diagnosis}

Across all four lines of work, two problems recur. \emph{Unbounded MR emergence}: every new domain or new program produces fresh MR formulations. \emph{Poor MR reusability}: identified MRs do not transport readily across programs that share deep structural similarities. Both problems follow from grounding MetaPatterns inductively. NOETHER replaces that inductive grounding with operator-algebraic grounding.
\paragraph{Relation to a separate line of work on minimum complete MR subsets.}
A separate line of work addresses the
\emph{orthogonal} problem of \emph{selecting} a minimum complete subset from a
\emph{given} metamorphic-relation pool: taking an MR set as input, it
characterises the smallest subset that preserves the pool's fault-detection
power under a fixed fault model, proves the corresponding decision problem
NP-hard, and provides approximation and exact (ILP) solvers. That work takes
the MR set as given and optimises its cardinality; the present paper is
concerned with the upstream question of where MRs and MetaPatterns
\emph{come from}: their constructive derivation from a program-induced
operator algebra and algebraic closure under \texttt{Translate}. The two are
complementary: NOETHER \emph{generates} the algebra-induced MR space that a
subset-selection procedure would then \emph{minimise}. No theorem or empirical
claim is shared: the present paper makes no minimality or subset-selection
claim, and the subset-selection work makes no derivation or closure claim.

%% NEW CHAPTER S3: NOETHER framework (theory consolidation, IMRaD)
%% ================================================================
\section{Proposed Method}
\label{sec:noether-framework}

This section presents NOETHER as an MR-identification method. The method takes a program-family governing equation/operator system as input, distils a program-induced operator algebra $\mathcal{A}_P$, decomposes the algebra into the five MetaPatterns, two family-layer refinements, and a relational extension, derives MetaPatterns and MR families from component invariants, and finally checks whether a concrete program interface exposes the controls and observations needed to instantiate an executable MR. The primary output is an \emph{identified MR family}; an executable MR instance is a downstream realization that may be blocked by missing interface affordances.

\paragraph{Counting rule used throughout the paper.}
Expert coverage is binary: an expert MR set covers a structural component if at least one expert MR belongs to that structural component. NOETHER coverage is also binary: NOETHER covers a structural component if the method explicitly derives at least one MR class from the program-family operator algebra in that structural component. Equation structure alone is not counted as coverage unless a corresponding MR class is written down. This rule is used before any empirical result is interpreted.

\paragraph{Status of formal objects.}
Definitions in this section fix the objects over which the claims are made: the program-induced operator algebra, structural component, MetaPattern, MR family, \texttt{Translate}, algebra-induced MR space, and MR mode. Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:seven-blocks} is empirical and refutable; it is not a theorem. Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}, Theorem~\ref{thm:decidable}, and Theorem~\ref{thm:ibt} are conditional results over those objects and the stated fault/signature classes. Theorem~$1'$ is the deliberately stronger absolute-completeness conjecture, and Section~\ref{subsec:negative-pwr} refutes it.

\paragraph{Running example.}
For the equivariant-ML instance, the family algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{equi}}$ contains an $E(3)$ group action on point-cloud inputs and an output representation on logits. CONSTRUCT-MP assigns this operator to $G$, derives the MetaPattern $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$, instantiates the MR family $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{inv}.\mathrm{eqv}}$, and produces an executable rotation MR $\rho_{\mathrm{rot}}$ when the interface exposes point coordinates and class logits. The same chain is used throughout: operator in $\mathcal{A}_P$ $\to$ structural component $\to$ MetaPattern $\to$ MR family $\to$ executable MR instance if the interface permits.

Operator-algebraic preliminaries and the structural decomposition appear in \S\ref{sec:prelim}; the algebra-induced metamorphic relation space, the CONSTRUCT-MP construction, the algebraic closure theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}), and the polynomial-time constructibility theorem (Theorem~\ref{thm:decidable}) in \S\ref{sec:framework}. The framework is then instantiated on three structurally distinct operator algebras: Boltzmann reactor physics in \S\ref{sec:reactor}, equivariant machine learning in \S\ref{sec:cross-domain}, and relational query optimisers in \S\ref{subsec:third-domain}. The section concludes by falsifying the strictly stronger absolute-completeness conjecture, Theorem~$1'$, on a fourth program family (PWR core diffusion) via two pairwise-independent counterexamples (\S\ref{subsec:negative-pwr}).

\subsection{Operator-algebraic preliminaries}
\label{sec:prelim}

This section introduces the algebraic apparatus used by NOETHER. We assume basic familiarity with group actions, equivalence classes, and quotient sets, but not with functional analysis. Each construct is defined at the level needed for the framework and later instantiated in reactor physics and equivariant machine learning.

We treat a program $P$ as a (possibly partial) computable function $P:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$, and a \emph{program-induced operator algebra} $\mathcal{A}_{\mathcal{F}}=(\mathcal{O},\circ,\sim_{\mathcal{F}})$ collects the operators acting on $\mathcal{X}$, $\mathcal{Y}$, or both, under a composition $\circ$ and a program-family equivalence $\sim_{\mathcal{F}}$. The decomposition below draws on eight structural-operator types, each defined formally in Appendix~\ref{app:operator-defs}: \emph{symmetry groups} ($G$: $P(g\cdot x)=\rho(g)\,P(x)$), \emph{order operators} ($O_{\le}$: monotonicity and linearity), \emph{self-adjoint operators} ($T^{*}$: $\langle Lx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ly\rangle$), \emph{time-reversal operators} ($\mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}$: anti-unitary involutions of a time coordinate), \emph{limit operators} ($\mathcal{L}^{*}$: parametrised convergence $\mathcal{L}_\theta\to\mathcal{L}_*$), the \emph{qualitative-dynamics} ($\mathcal{D}^{*}$) and \emph{method-comparison} ($\mathcal{E}^{*}$) refinements, and the relational-equivalence extension ($\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$, Definition~\ref{def:b-rel}).

\subsubsection{Decomposition of an operator algebra}
\label{subsec:decomposition}

Given $\mathcal{A}_P = (\mathcal{O}, \circ, \sim_{\mathcal{F}})$, we decompose $\mathcal{O}$ into the five MetaPatterns, two refinements, and a relational extension introduced above:
$$\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P) = \bigl(\,G,\; O_{\le},\; T^{*},\; \mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}},\; \mathcal{L}^{*},\; \mathcal{D}^{*},\; \mathcal{E}^{*},\; \mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}\,\bigr),$$
where $G$ collects symmetry subgroups, $O_{\le}$ monotone and linear operators, $T^{*}$ self-adjoint operators, $\mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}$ time-reversal operators, $\mathcal{L}^{*}$ limit operators, $\mathcal{D}^{*}$ qualitative-dynamics operators, $\mathcal{E}^{*}$ method-comparison operators, and $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ relational-equivalence operators. We call these eight units the \emph{structural components} of $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)$; the first five ($G$, $O_{\le}$, $T^{*}$, $\mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}$, $\mathcal{L}^{*}$) are the MetaPatterns, and the remaining three are the two refinements ($\mathcal{D}^{*}$, $\mathcal{E}^{*}$) and the relational extension ($\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$).

Conservation laws are not an additional MetaPattern: by the Noether-style correspondence between symmetries and conserved quantities, a conservation/invariance relation is the $G$ MetaPattern $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$. When evaluation tables record conservation separately, they record the MR family $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{inv}.\mathrm{con}}$ under $G$, not a sixth MetaPattern.

\begin{definition}[Relational-equivalence extension]
\label{def:b-rel}
A \emph{relational-equivalence operator} is a binary relation $\equiv_{\mathcal{R}}$ on expressions over an idempotent semiring $(\mathcal{S}, \oplus, \otimes, \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{1})$ such that $E \equiv_{\mathcal{R}} E'$ iff $E$ and $E'$ are equal under all valid evaluation contexts of $\mathcal{S}$, generated by a finite set $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rel}} = \{\mathcal{R}_1, \dots, \mathcal{R}_K\}$ of identity-preserving rewriting rules, each $\mathcal{R}_i$ an ordered pair $(\mathrm{lhs}_i, \mathrm{rhs}_i)$ of semiring expressions with the property $\mathrm{eval}(\mathrm{lhs}_i, D) =_{\mathrm{bag}} \mathrm{eval}(\mathrm{rhs}_i, D)$ on every valid input $D$. The relational extension $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ collects all such operators. It is empty for program families without idempotent-semiring rewriting structure (Boltzmann reactor physics, equivariant ML) and non-empty for those with it (relational query optimisers, \S\ref{subsec:third-domain}).
\end{definition}

\paragraph{Necessity and empirical status.} We do not claim the eight structural components are necessary in an absolute sense or exhaustive; they are an \emph{empirical curation} of mathematical structures that recur across the program families we have studied, currently sufficient for these families but not provably necessary in general. This is NOETHER's main upstream limitation. Induction is not eliminated but moved one level up, from ``what MetaPatterns recur in observed MRs?'' to ``what algebraic structures recur across program families?'', after which the downstream derivation of $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ is mechanical and provably closed (Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}). We state this sufficiency as an explicit empirical hypothesis with a documented out-of-scope catalogue.

\begin{hypothesis}[Decomposition sufficiency]
\label{hyp:seven-blocks}
Let $P$ be a program belonging to a program family $\mathcal{F}$ whose semantics admit an operator-algebraic representation $\mathcal{A}_P$ over (i) finite or finite-dimensional symmetry groups, (ii) partial orders with monotone or linear operators, (iii) self-adjoint operators with respect to a fixed inner product, (iv) anti-unitary involutions of a time coordinate, (v) limit operations of analytical (mesh-refinement, parameter-perturbation, or asymptotic) type, (vi) qualitative-dynamics attractors of an underlying ordinary-differential-equation / partial-differential-equation (ODE/PDE) system, (vii) inter-method comparison partial orders, and (viii) identity-preserving rewriting rule sets on an idempotent semiring. For such families the structural decomposition
$$\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P) = G \,\dot\cup\, O_{\le} \,\dot\cup\, T^{*} \,\dot\cup\, \mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}} \,\dot\cup\, \mathcal{L}^{*} \,\dot\cup\, \mathcal{D}^{*} \,\dot\cup\, \mathcal{E}^{*} \,\dot\cup\, \mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$$
is sufficient: every operator in $\mathcal{A}_P$ relevant to MR derivation is assigned to at least one MetaPattern, refinement, or the relational extension. Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:seven-blocks} is an empirical hypothesis open to refutation.
\end{hypothesis}

\begin{remark}[Single-class instances]
\label{rem:single-class-instances}
For the three instantiated algebras we adopt a canonical $\pi$-template per non-empty structural component under which $|\mathcal{I}_s/\sim_s|=1$ (e.g.\ Boltzmann's $G$ MetaPattern is a single $\sim_s$ class covering both geometric quarter-rotations and energy-group permutations), so $|\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)|$ equals the number of non-empty structural components per instance; a finer treatment (Step~3 of CONSTRUCT-MP) would split the corresponding MetaPattern.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Decomposition sufficiency vs.\ \texttt{Translate} sufficiency]
\label{rem:block-vs-translate}
Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:seven-blocks} asserts the structural components suffice to \emph{assign} every relevant operator, not that every MR over $\mathcal{A}_P$ is \texttt{Translate}-reachable from a single component invariant. The negative PWR result (\S\ref{subsec:negative-pwr}) exhibits two MRs whose operators are assigned to components yet whose content is not in $\mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PWR}})$, so \texttt{Translate}'s expressive form is a second, independent constraint beyond the decomposition.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Known and conjectured out-of-scope program families]
\label{rem:counterex}
The hypothesis is open to refutation. Six families are known or conjectured to fall outside its image and to require an additional MetaPattern: (i)~symplectic systems; (ii)~sheaf-theoretic / categorical constructions; (iii)~probabilistic / martingale invariants; (iv)~topological invariants; (v)~label-consistency for supervised learning (empirically witnessed by the \S\ref{subsec:case-study} cat-(i) wrong-sign $0/5$); and (vi)~empirical parameter-distribution divergence (witnessed by the \S\ref{subsec:deepcrime-pilot} pilot's undetected cat-v-02/04/05). Each signals a candidate additional MetaPattern, to be admitted when the program family demands it; one (metric-stability $M_{\mathrm{lip}}$) has an explicit \texttt{Translate}-template design (Remark~\ref{rem:metric-stability-block}), and Appendix~\ref{app:out-of-scope} catalogues concrete out-of-scope MRs.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Domain-level out-of-scope]
\label{rem:domain-out-of-scope}
In addition to the candidate-additional-MetaPattern families of Remark~\ref{rem:counterex}, four program-family classes are out of scope for NOETHER in its present form because they admit no operator-algebraic representation at all: general web applications, reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback (RLHF) reward models / LLM agents, distributed-consensus protocols, and compiler-internal optimisations. NOETHER's reach is therefore consistent with its scope precondition: systems under test (SUTs) from textbook-codified mathematical, physical, or relational-algebra domains are within reach, those from general software-engineering domains without such codification are not.
\end{remark}

\begin{remark}[Metric-stability candidate additional MetaPattern, $M_{\mathrm{lip}}$]
\label{rem:metric-stability-block}
The most concrete candidate additional MetaPattern (Remark~\ref{rem:counterex}) is metric-stability: $M_{\mathrm{lip}}$ is the family of $K$-Lipschitz maps $(\mathcal{X}, d_{\mathcal{X}})\to(\mathcal{Y}, d_{\mathcal{Y}})$, with induced MetaPattern $m_{\mathrm{lip}}$ the class of pointwise stability inequalities $d_{\mathcal{Y}}(P(x'), P(x))\le K\,d_{\mathcal{X}}(x', x)$ and a \texttt{Translate} template that perturbs $x'=x+\varepsilon u$ ($\|u\|=1$, $|\varepsilon|<\delta$) and predicates a $K$-Lipschitz output bound. It would sit after $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ in the canonical ordering (metric structure is independent of the eight existing component invariants), and Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}'s proof transfers since $m_{\mathrm{lip}}$ is single-MetaPattern. We do not commit to it as canonical here; it is the empirical orphan of the \S\ref{subsec:reactor-mapping} audit, recorded in Appendix~\ref{app:out-of-scope}.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{The two-layer model: five MetaPatterns and ten MR families, and MR mode}
\label{subsec:generator-family}

The model has two layers. Layer~1 (L1) is the set of \emph{MetaPatterns}: five canonical structures on the solution space, each the program-level image of one algebraic structure (a group action, a partial order, a self-adjoint operator, a time-reversal involution, and a parametrised limit). Layer~2 (L2) is the set of \emph{MR families}: the ten executable relations a test engineer enumerates, each instantiating one MetaPattern. Making the two layers explicit controls both how the decomposition is instantiated as executable tests and how detection independence is read.

\paragraph{Layer 1: the five MetaPatterns.} The MetaPattern set is $\{G,\,O_{\le},\,T^{*},\,\mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}},\,\mathcal{L}^{*}\}$ (symmetry, order, self-adjointness, time reversal, and limits). Formally, each MetaPattern is the equivalence class of algebra-induced MRs that CONSTRUCT-MP derives from one such structure, named by the invariant it preserves: $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$ (Invariance) from $G$, $m_{\mathrm{mono}}$ (Monotonicity) from $O_{\le}$, $m_{\mathrm{adj}}$ (Adjoint) from $T^{*}$, $m_{\mathrm{rev}}$ (Reversal) from $\mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}}$, and $m_{\mathrm{conv}}$ (Convergence) from $\mathcal{L}^{*}$. (The genus name \emph{Adjoint} for $m_{\mathrm{adj}}$ is kept distinct from the child MR family $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{adj}.\mathrm{self}}$.) Two further structures are refinements of these MetaPatterns rather than additional MetaPatterns, and they enter the model at Layer~2 as MR families. Qualitative dynamics $\mathcal{D}^{*}$ refines $O_{\le}$: bounded-variation, no-overshoot, and Sturm-type oscillation invariants are order relations on a trajectory rather than on pointwise values (sharpened by $T^{*}$ where the operator is Sturm--Liouville). Method comparison $\mathcal{E}^{*}$ refines $\mathcal{L}^{*}$: an accuracy partial order $M_1 \preceq M_2$ is an order on a family of approximants converging to the same limit. Representation-invariance under $\mathcal{L}^{*}$ specialises, in the exact idempotent-semiring case, to relational equivalence $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$, which lies outside the Lie-group / self-adjoint / time-reversal core. Conservation remains the Noether image of $G$ (the $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$ entry of Table~\ref{tab:refinement}), not a separate MetaPattern. This two-layer reading is a presentation of the same decomposition, not a new hypothesis: the sufficiency claim (Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:seven-blocks}) and the closure and decidability results (Theorems~\ref{thm:closure}, \ref{thm:decidable}) are unchanged.

\paragraph{Layer 2: the ten MR families.} An \emph{MR family} is the set of executable MRs obtained by instantiating one MetaPattern from $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ under a fixed $\pi$-template and a chosen MR mode (Definition~\ref{def:mr-mode}); it is the unit a test engineer enumerates and one row of the empirical coverage matrix (\S\ref{para:real-bug-protocol}). Table~\ref{tab:mr-families} lists the ten families used in this paper. Each family is written $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{parent}.\mathrm{child}}$: a sans-serif family glyph whose subscript names its parent MetaPattern (before the dot) and the instantiating mechanism (after), so the parent is recoverable from the symbol; this glyph is tier-distinct from the MetaPattern symbol $m_{\bullet}$ and the executable-MR symbol $\rho_{\bullet}$. The map from the five MetaPatterns to the ten families is one-to-many and program-family-dependent (Figure~\ref{fig:two-layer-map}); which families are non-empty is determined by $\mathcal{A}_P$. A single MetaPattern may produce several families (the $G$ MetaPattern $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$ produces both the equivariance family and, by the Noether correspondence of \S\ref{subsec:decomposition}, the conservation family), consistent with Step~3 of CONSTRUCT-MP and Remark~\ref{rem:single-class-instances}. The chain is therefore the two layers: MetaPatterns (L1) $\to$ MR families (L2); the family layer refines the MetaPattern set rather than introducing a parallel taxonomy.

\paragraph{MR mode: input-orbit versus implementation-orbit.} An MR tests a compatibility law by varying one of two axes while holding the other fixed.

\begin{definition}[MR mode]
\label{def:mr-mode}
A \emph{Mode-I} (input-orbit) MR fixes a single implementation $P$ and varies the input along the MetaPattern structure: $R(P;\,x,\,t(x))$ with $t$ a group action, a mesh refinement, or a time reversal. A \emph{Mode-M} (implementation-orbit) MR fixes a single input and varies the implementation among realisations $P^{(1)},\dots,P^{(k)}$ of the same ideal operator (different methods, drivers, storage layouts, or parallelisations): $R(P^{(1)},\dots,P^{(k)};\,x)$. A Mode-M MR is a relative oracle: a violation localises the fault to the disagreeing set rather than to a single realisation, so localisation needs an additional discriminator (a third method, a control input on which the realisations must agree, or pre/post version closure).
\end{definition}

\paragraph{Fault classes and detection independence.} Each family $R_i$ tests one compatibility law and, by the Invariance-Blindness reading (Theorem~\ref{thm:ibt} for $G$ and $T^{*}$), detects exactly the faults that break it. $R_i$ \emph{independently distinguishes} its fault class when some fault is detected by $R_i$ and no other family (a unique-detection witness). Each family of Table~\ref{tab:mr-families} carries such a witness, including at least one non-crash fault, in the corpus of \S\ref{para:real-bug-protocol}. This is witness-level necessity, not pairwise orthogonality (families sharing a MetaPattern may co-fire), and the minimal detecting subset is deferred to future work (\S\ref{sec:future-work}).

\subsection{Deriving MR classes with CONSTRUCT-MP}
\label{sec:framework}

\subsubsection{Algebra-induced metamorphic relations}

Before defining algebra-induced MRs we make explicit the \texttt{Translate} operator that converts a single component invariant into an executable MR. Without this definition, the closure result of Theorem~\ref{thm:closure} would quantify over an undefined construct.

\begin{definition}[Component invariant]
\label{def:block-invariant}
Let $s \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ be one of the eight structural components. A \emph{component invariant of $\mathcal{A}_P$ under $s$} is a pair $\iota = (\Phi, \pi)$ where $\Phi$ is a finite set of operators drawn from $s$, and $\pi$ is a relation $\pi \subseteq (\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y})^k$ for some arity $k \ge 1$ such that for every $P \in \mathcal{F}$ and every choice of operators $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_n \in \Phi$, the tuple $\bigl((x_i, P(x_i))\bigr)_{i=1}^k$ obtained by applying $\phi_1, \dots, \phi_n$ to a base input $x \in \mathcal{X}$ in the canonical order specified by $s$ satisfies $\pi$. We write $\mathcal{I}_s$ for the set of component invariants under $s$ and $\sim_s$ for the equivalence relation $\iota \sim_s \iota'$ iff $\Phi = \Phi'$ and $\pi$, $\pi'$ define the same constraint up to relabelling of input/output coordinates.
\end{definition}

The relation $\sim_s$ is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive by construction (set equality and constraint equality are equivalence relations); hence $\sim_s$ is a genuine equivalence relation on $\mathcal{I}_s$, justifying the quotient in Step 3 of CONSTRUCT-MP below.

\begin{definition}[\texttt{Translate}]
\label{def:translate}
The \texttt{Translate} operator is the function
\[
\mathrm{Translate}: \mathcal{I}_s \times \{s\} \;\longrightarrow\; \mathrm{MR}(P)
\]
that maps a component invariant $\iota = (\Phi, \pi)$ under structural component $s$ to the metamorphic relation
\[
\rho_{\iota,s}: \quad \forall x \in \mathcal{X},\ \forall \phi_1, \dots, \phi_n \in \Phi : \quad \pi\bigl((x_i,\, P(x_i))_{i=1}^k\bigr) \text{ holds},
\]
where the input tuple $(x_i)_{i=1}^k$ is generated by applying the $\phi_j$ in the canonical order specified by $s$ (the convention is fixed per structural component: e.g., for $s = G$, $x_i = g_i \cdot x_0$ with $g_i$ enumerated by group orbit; for $s = T^{*}$, the tuple ranges over the two arguments of the inner product). \texttt{Translate} is well-defined because (i) the per-structural-component canonical order resolves any ambiguity in tuple generation, and (ii) $\sim_s$-equivalent invariants are mapped to MRs that are $\sim$-equivalent as logical statements over $P$. Per-structural-component instantiations of \texttt{Translate} are tabulated in Appendix~\ref{app:translate-table}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Algebra-induced MR]
\label{def:alg-induced}
Let $\mathcal{A}_P$ be a program-induced operator algebra and let $\rho$ be an MR over a program $P$. We say $\rho$ is \emph{induced by $\mathcal{A}_P$}, written $\rho \in \mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_P)$, when there exist (i) a structural component $s \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)$, (ii) a component invariant $\iota \in \mathcal{I}_s$, and (iii) the equality $\rho = \mathrm{Translate}(\iota, s)$ holds in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:translate}. Properties of $P$ that constrain executions but cannot be obtained as $\mathrm{Translate}(\iota, s)$ for any single structural component $s$ and any invariant $\iota \in \mathcal{I}_s$ are \emph{not} algebra-induced in this sense; concrete examples are catalogued in Appendix~\ref{app:out-of-scope}.
\end{definition}

\subsubsection{Construction of the MetaPattern set}

We present the deductive procedure CONSTRUCT-MP that maps an algebra-decomposition to a MetaPattern set.

\begin{description}
  \item[Step 1: Invariant extraction.] For each structural component $s$ in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)$, compute the set of invariants $\mathcal{I}_s$ of $\mathcal{A}_P$ under $s$.
  \item[Step 2: MR derivation.] For each invariant $\iota \in \mathcal{I}_s$, derive the MR family $\mathcal{R}(\iota) = \{\,\rho \in \mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_P) \mid \rho = \mathrm{Translate}(\iota', s),\; \iota' \sim_s \iota\,\}$.
  \item[Step 3: Quotient (per equivalence class).] For each $\sim_s$-equivalence class $[\iota] \in \mathcal{I}_s/\sim_s$, form the MetaPattern $m_{s,[\iota]} = \mathcal{R}(\iota)$.
  \item[Step 4: Aggregation.] Return $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P) = \bigcup_{s \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)} \{\, m_{s,[\iota]} : [\iota] \in \mathcal{I}_s/\sim_s \,\}$, so $|\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)| = \sum_s |\mathcal{I}_s/\sim_s| \ge $ the number of non-empty structural components.
\end{description}

The four steps are intentionally stated as a textual algorithm; the supplementary package includes the corresponding implementation sketch.

\begin{remark}[MetaPattern granularity]
\label{rem:mp-per-class}
Each MetaPattern $m_{s,[\iota]}$ corresponds to a single $\sim_s$-equivalence class of invariants in structural component $s$. A structural component carrying $k_s > 1$ such classes (for instance geometric quarter-rotations and energy-group permutations within $G$ on $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{Boltz}}$, when treated as separate $\sim_s$ classes) contributes $k_s$ distinct MetaPatterns. In the three instances of \S\S\ref{sec:reactor}--\ref{subsec:third-domain} we group invariants within a structural component under a single $\sim_s$-equivalence class (a single canonical $\pi$-template per non-empty structural component; see Remark~\ref{rem:single-class-instances}), so $|\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_{P})|$ equals the number of non-empty structural components in those instances. The Invariance-Blindness analysis (\S\ref{subsec:ibt}) applies directly to each $m_{s,[\iota]}$ at its native per-class granularity.
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Algebraic closure under Translate, the canonical MetaPattern ordering, and out-of-scope MRs}
\label{subsec:completeness}

\begin{definition}[Canonical MetaPattern ordering]
\label{def:canonical-order}
We adopt the strict total order on structural components
$$G > O_{\le} > T^{*} > \mathcal{T}^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}} > \mathcal{L}^{*} > \mathcal{D}^{*} > \mathcal{E}^{*} > \mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}.$$
An MR derivable through multiple structural components is assigned to the highest-priority structural component in this order. The placement of $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ at the bottom reflects its semiring-rewriting nature, which sits algebraically downstream of the non-relational structural components: rewriting equivalences typically depend on the program family's input-perturbation, order, and method-comparison structure rather than the converse.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Algebraic Closure under \texttt{Translate}]
\label{thm:closure}
Let $\mathcal{A}_P$ be a program-induced operator algebra with decomposition $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ as in Section~\ref{subsec:decomposition}, and let $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P) = \mathrm{CONSTRUCT\textnormal{-}MP}(\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P))$. Then for every $\rho \in \mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ in the sense of Definition~\ref{def:alg-induced}, there exists a unique $m \in \mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ such that $\rho \in m$, where uniqueness is determined under the canonical MetaPattern ordering.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}[Scope of Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}]
\label{rem:scope}
Theorem~\ref{thm:closure} is a closure statement, not a completeness claim over arbitrary properties one might assert about $P$'s executions. It quantifies over $\mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ as defined by Definition~\ref{def:alg-induced}, namely the algebra-induced MRs reachable through the \texttt{Translate} operator from a single component invariant. Three concrete classes of MRs lie outside this scope and are not covered by the theorem; they are documented in Appendix~\ref{app:out-of-scope}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{Probabilistic MRs without operator-algebraic representation}: e.g.\ MRs that constrain output \emph{distributions} (such as ``the entropy of $f(\mathbf{x})$ should not decrease under input augmentation $A$'') when the augmentation is not expressible as an operator in $\mathcal{O}$.
    \item \emph{Input-distribution MRs} not expressible over $\mathcal{A}_P$ operators: e.g.\ adversarial-perturbation MRs ``$\| \delta\|_p \le \epsilon \Rightarrow f(\mathbf{x}+\delta) = f(\mathbf{x})$'' whose perturbation set is not a group action on $\mathcal{X}$.
    \item \emph{Compositional MRs spanning multiple structural components under non-\texttt{Translate} derivations}: MRs requiring simultaneous use of two component invariants in a way that is not the canonical-MetaPattern-ordering reduction of Definition~\ref{def:canonical-order}.
\end{enumerate}
The strictly stronger statement that every MR formulable as a property over $\mathcal{A}_P$'s operators (without restricting to \texttt{Translate}-reachable derivations) is contained in some $m \in \mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ is identified as Theorem~1$'$ in Appendix~\ref{app:proofs}. Section~\ref{subsec:negative-pwr} and Appendix~\ref{app:negative-proofs} establish that this stronger statement is false on the PWR core diffusion algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PWR}}$, by exhibiting two concrete counterexamples ($\rho_{\mathrm{nonadd}}$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{MTC\text{-}bor}}$, where MTC denotes moderator temperature coefficient) whose obstructions identify five structurally independent extensions of \texttt{Translate}'s signature. The combined open problem (whether such an extended \texttt{Translate} preserves Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}'s closure and Theorem~\ref{thm:decidable}'s polynomial-time constructibility) is the principal open question for follow-up work.
\end{remark}

A sceptical reading might object that the by-construction status of Theorem~\ref{thm:closure} makes it near-tautological. We acknowledge that the closure result is by-construction within the explicit scope of Definition~\ref{def:alg-induced} (which fixes $\mathrm{MR}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ as the \texttt{Translate}-image of $\mathcal{A}_P$). The substantive value lies in what the theorem then enables: Theorem~\ref{thm:closure} converts an empirical-adequacy claim (``our pattern grid covers $X\%$ of observed MRs'') into a structural-adequacy claim (``our pattern grid is exhaustive of the algebra-induced MR space, modulo the explicit out-of-scope classes of Remark~\ref{rem:scope}''). Empirical adequacy frameworks built on inductive pattern grids do not guarantee algebraic closure even in this bounded sense; NOETHER guarantees it, and the obligation imposed on any user of the framework is then to verify that no \texttt{Translate}-reachable MR is dropped by CONSTRUCT-MP, a verification that is mechanical once the algebraic input has been fixed.

The theorem still imposes a checkable obligation on the framework. If an MR is induced by an invariant in $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ but cannot be assigned by CONSTRUCT-MP, then at least one component (invariant extraction, $\mathrm{Translate}$, structural equivalence, or the canonical ordering) is underspecified. Thus the result is not an empirical coverage claim; it is a well-formedness and closure guarantee for the downstream construction once the algebraic input has been fixed. The framework's additional theoretical results complement Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}: Theorem~\ref{thm:decidable} bounds the construction's polynomial-time complexity under a finite generating set; Theorem~$1'$ (Conjecture~\ref{conj:absolute}), which makes the stronger claim of absolute completeness over arbitrary properties expressible in $\mathcal{A}_P$, is falsified on $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{PWR}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:negative-pwr}); the falsification identifies five structural obstructions in \texttt{Translate}'s signature (Appendix~\ref{app:negative-proofs}), with five further candidate dimensions surveyed on $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{equi}}$ and $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:third-domain}).

\begin{remark}[Scope for the relational extension $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$]
\label{rem:closure-brel}
Theorem~\ref{thm:closure}'s closure extends to $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ when the rewriting rule set $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ is finite (e.g.\ the heuristic-rewrite normal forms of TPC-H-class queries~\cite{Wang2024QED, Zhou2022SPES}); unbounded recursive rewriting (non-terminating Datalog) is out of scope (Remark~\ref{rem:counterex}).
\end{remark}

\subsubsection{Complexity and decidability}
\label{subsec:decidability}

\begin{theorem}[Complexity of CONSTRUCT-MP under a finite generating set]
\label{thm:decidable}
Suppose $\mathcal{A}_P$ admits a finite generating set $\mathrm{gen}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ of cardinality $n$, with each generator's invariant computation \emph{assumed to terminate} in time $t_i$. Then $\mathbb{M}(\mathcal{A}_P)$ is computable in time $O\!\bigl(\,n \cdot \max_i t_i \cdot \log n\,\bigr)$. This is a complexity bound on the construction rather than a decidability result: termination of per-structural-component invariant extraction is assumed within $t_i$, and for the relational extension $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ general query equivalence is undecidable, so only the fixed-rule-set fragment is covered (Remark~\ref{rem:decidable-brel}). The factors $t_i$ absorb the realised per-generator invariant cost: for a finite symmetry group the relevant $t_i$ can scale with the group order $|G|$, which may itself grow exponentially in the number of generators (for example $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^{k}$ has $|G| = 2^{k}$), so the bound is polynomial in $n$ and the realised generator costs (output-sensitive) rather than necessarily polynomial in a compact group presentation.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}[Decidability for $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ under a fixed rule set]
\label{rem:decidable-brel}
The polynomial-time bound holds for $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ under a fixed rule set $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{rel}}$: although first-order/bag-semantics query equivalence is undecidable in general, equivalence under a fixed rule set is decidable and SMT-verifiable on substantial benchmark fractions~\cite{Wang2024QED, Zhou2022SPES}.
\end{remark}

\paragraph{Per-structural-component cost.} The per-generator invariant-extraction cost is $O(|G|^2)$ for finite symmetry groups, $O(d_G^2)$ over the Lie-algebra basis for finite-dimensional Lie groups (e.g.\ $\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $d_G=3$), and polynomial in a user-supplied truncation $K$ for finitely-generated infinite-discrete groups; the per-structural-component breakdown and the infinite-group truncation discussion are in supplementary~S1. For a finite group $|G|$ may grow exponentially in the number of generators (e.g.\ $(\mathbb{Z}_2)^k$ has $|G|=2^k$), so Theorem~\ref{thm:decidable}'s bound is output-sensitive in the realised generator costs rather than polynomial in a compact group presentation.

\subsubsection{The principal limitation}

NOETHER replaces inductive grounding with algebraic grounding \emph{downstream of $\mathcal{A}_P$}. Upstream, the distillation of $\mathcal{A}_P$ from a program family remains a human task. This limitation is central to the framework's scope: NOETHER does not automate domain modelling, but it turns the step after domain modelling into a well-defined construction. A second limitation, made explicit in \S\ref{subsec:negative-pwr} and Appendix~\ref{app:negative-proofs}, is that even when $\mathcal{A}_P$ is fully specified, \texttt{Translate}'s present signature (single-component, first-order $\pi$-template, single partial-order direction, operating on $P(x)$ tuples rather than on operator-spectrum quantities) systematically excludes a class of MRs that engineering practice treats as standard: non-additivity of operator-composition functionals and higher-order mixed parametric dependences. The principal limitation is therefore twofold: the upstream distillation of $\mathcal{A}_P$, and the present signature of \texttt{Translate}.

The downstream layer is mechanical: Theorem~\ref{thm:closure} (algebraic closure under \texttt{Translate}) and Theorem~\ref{thm:decidable} (polynomial-time constructibility) operate on a given structural decomposition. The upstream layer remains empirical: the structural decomposition is Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:seven-blocks}, an open empirical hypothesis with six documented out-of-scope program-family classes (Remark~\ref{rem:counterex}). Theorem~1$'$ (absolute completeness) is open. Sections~\ref{sec:reactor}, \ref{sec:cross-domain}, and \ref{subsec:third-domain} instantiate NOETHER on three structurally distinct program families.

\subsection{Boltzmann instantiation: from transport to diffusion to burnup}
\label{sec:reactor}

This section instantiates NOETHER on the Boltzmann transport equation and traces the construction through neutron transport, diffusion, and burnup.

\subsubsection{The Boltzmann program family and its operator algebra}

The Boltzmann transport equation governs the distribution of neutral particles. In its time-independent eigenvalue form for fission systems:
\begin{multline}
\hat{\Omega}\!\cdot\!\nabla\psi(\vec{r},\hat{\Omega},E) + \Sigma_t(\vec{r},E)\psi \\
= \int\!\!\int \Sigma_s(\vec{r}, E'\!\to\!E,\hat{\Omega}'\!\to\!\hat{\Omega})\,\psi\,dE'd\hat{\Omega}'
+ \tfrac{1}{k}\,\chi(E)\!\!\int\!\nu\Sigma_f(\vec{r},E')\psi\,dE'.
\end{multline}

The program-induced operator algebra $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{Boltz}}$ contains
\[
\{G_{\mathrm{geom}},\, \mathfrak{R}_E,\, \mathcal{L}_{\Sigma},\,
\mathcal{L}_\nu,\, \mathcal{L}^*,\, \mathcal{T},\, \mathcal{L}_h,\,
\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{Bate}},\, \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{cmp}}\}.
\]
Decomposed along the eight structural components of Section~\ref{subsec:decomposition}, $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{Boltz}}$ has entries in seven structural components (with $\mathcal{B}^{*}_{\mathrm{rel}}$ empty under the absence of idempotent-semiring rewriting structure). Every operator listed has an unambiguous status in the established theory of neutral-particle transport~\cite{BellGlasstone1970, LewisMiller1993}.

\subsubsection{Running CONSTRUCT-MP on \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{Boltz}}$}{A\_Boltz}}

Steps 1--4 of CONSTRUCT-MP produce five MetaPatterns: $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$ (invariance/equivariance), $m_{\mathrm{mono}}$ (parameter-monotonicity), $m_{\mathrm{adj}}$ (self-adjoint duality / adjoint reciprocity), $m_{\mathrm{rev}}$ (time-reversal compatibility), and $m_{\mathrm{conv}}$ (discretisation convergence), together with two MR families that refine them: $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{mono}.\mathrm{shape}}$ (qualitative-dynamics shape invariants, refining $m_{\mathrm{mono}}$) and $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{conv}.\mathrm{rate}}$ (method-comparison error-bound partial orders, refining $m_{\mathrm{conv}}$).

\subsubsection{PWR corpus placement under canonical symbols}
\label{subsec:reactor-mapping}

\paragraph{Provenance and scope of the PWR corpus.}
The reactor-physics material used here is a PWR MR corpus distilled from standard reactor-physics literature~\cite{BellGlasstone1970, LewisMiller1993} (supplementary~S2), not an independent external benchmark. It tests vocabulary coherence: whether reactor-domain MRs can be placed in the same canonical symbol system used throughout the paper. External-transfer evidence (a PARCS V\&V or IAEA-TECDOC-class catalogue) and the reactor-side analogue of the commons-math cross-codebase pilot are committed as follow-up (supplementary~S4/S5).

The PWR corpus contains five recurring property groups: conservation/invariance, monotonicity, convergence, qualitative trajectory shape, and method-accuracy/bounding. We use these groups only as source material for canonical placement, not as a second MetaPattern vocabulary. Table~\ref{tab:refinement} maps each reactor property group to either one of the five MetaPatterns or a named MR family in Table~\ref{tab:mr-families}. The same placement also exposes two reactor structures, adjoint reciprocity and collisionless reversibility, that belong to the canonical grid even when a compact engineering MR set does not isolate them.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Reactor-physics property groups are placed under canonical NOETHER symbols.}
\label{tab:refinement}
\small
\begin{tabular}{p{0.25\textwidth} p{0.24\textwidth} p{0.41\textwidth}}
\toprule
\textbf{Reactor property group} & \textbf{Canonical symbol} & \textbf{Placement} \\
\midrule
Conservation / invariance & $G \mapsto \mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{inv}.\mathrm{con}}$ & Conserved quantities are the Noether image of the symmetry MetaPattern $m_{\mathrm{inv}}$. \\
Monotonicity & $O_{\le} \mapsto \mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{mono}.\mathrm{stat}}$ & Order-preserving perturbations instantiate the static-order family. \\
Convergence & $\mathcal{L}^{*} \mapsto \mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{conv}.\mathrm{lim}}$ & Mesh, time-step, or fixed-point refinement instantiates the convergence family. \\

\end{table}

For example, eight of the eighteen supplementary PWR MRs instantiate $G$, $O_{\le}$, or $\mathcal{L}^{*}$ directly; six instantiate the family-layer refinements $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{mono}.\mathrm{shape}}$ and $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{conv}.\mathrm{rate}}$; and three instantiate $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{adj}.\mathrm{dual}}$ or $\mathsf{f}_{\mathrm{rev}.\mathrm{traj}}$. The last MR (mixed temperature coefficient under boron concentration) is correctly left outside the current decomposition and becomes the candidate metric-stability/second-order-interaction extension discussed in Appendix~\ref{app:out-of-scope}. The gain is canonical placement: reactor-specific property groups are read through the same MetaPattern and MR-family symbols used for equivariant ML, relational optimisers, and the empirical evidence tables.

\paragraph{Element-wise correspondence.} Supplementary~S2 traces representative reactor-physics MRs from the standard literature~\cite{BellGlasstone1970, LewisMiller1993} to their NOETHER placement, including source equations and \texttt{Translate} templates. The main text keeps only the property-group mapping because Table~\ref{tab:refinement} is the level at which the symbol system is introduced.

\paragraph{Noether-style derivation and specialisations.} Appendix~\ref{app:noether-deriv} gives a worked Noether-style derivation of $m_{\mathrm{adj}}$ from the Boltzmann bilinear form $\mathcal{F}[\phi,\phi^{\dagger}]$, derives the adjoint-reciprocity MR $\rho_{\mathrm{adj}}$, and specialises the MetaPattern set to neutron transport, diffusion, and burnup solvers.

\subsubsection{Summary}
NOETHER applied to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{Boltz}}$ deductively produces the same five-MetaPattern grid used elsewhere in the paper and populates it with reactor-specific MR families. All placements correspond to invariants independently validated in standard reactor-physics literature (symmetry-of-criticality and adjoint-perturbation theory~\cite{BellGlasstone1970}, cross-section monotonicity and collisionless time-reversal~\cite{LewisMiller1993}, adjoint-flux treatment~\cite{StammlerAbbate1983}). The contribution is therefore not de-novo discovery; these invariants are textbook-canonical. The contribution is the algebraic warrant for treating them as a uniform MetaPattern/MR-family grid. The next section turns to a more demanding case: a domain in which such an MR corpus does not yet exist.
